item.title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Times of Societal Polarization, Politicization, and Securitization
item.content:encoded:
Dorothee Maria Winkler, Bern University of Applied Sciences

David Risi, Bern University of Applied Sciences

Christopher Wickert, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Onna Malou van den Broek, Copenhagen Business School

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has a long and influential history as one of the dominant paradigms in managing the business-society interface. For years, CSR has served as the normative and strategic blueprint for companies in managing growing societal expectations such as climate change, corruption, and inequality, fundamentally shaping corporate behavior across sustainability, ethics, and stakeholder engagement. Over the past decade, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria seemed to be moving from the periphery to the center of attention for companies, and the formalization and legalization of CSR-related criteria have reinforced the importance of corporate responsibility and consolidated its position as a central area of concern for business firms.

However, after a long period of broad consensus on the desirability of business responsibility, the global political, social, and economic landscape has shifted in ways that fundamentally challenge the taken-for-granted position of CSR and related ideas about the role of business in society. These shifts occur amid widespread societal polarization, in which democratic countries face a profound sociocultural struggle between contending conservative and progressive visions, contributing to the erosion of democratic norms. We observe an active dismantling of CSR alongside the contraction and de-institutionalization of moral markets. As a result, CSR and sustainability have become highly polarized, reflecting broader political conflicts over the role of business in society.

The consequences of these developments are visible in corporate behavior. Businesses have begun to withdraw from seemingly firm commitments to sustainability and are recalibrating their strategies and operational activities. Leading firms, including major U.S. Big Tech companies such as Meta and Amazon, have rolled back or abandoned diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives almost overnight, potentially to align with shifting political priorities. U.S. firms increasingly adopt a reverse CSR approach, curtailing DEI efforts to appease political leadership or engaging in symbolic acts of proximity to power. Concepts such as "greenhushing"—the deliberate under-communication of CSR activities to avoid public and political attention—are once again becoming more important.

Overall, we witness the rise of populist and nationalist movements across Western democracies that eroded the political consensus and Zeitgeist supporting corporate responsibility frameworks. Alongside polarization, geopolitical tensions such as the persistence of violent conflicts like the Russia-Ukraine war and the escalation of competition among major economic and political powers have shifted state and corporate priorities away from shared responsibility toward national interests and security concerns. For instance, in November 2025, the European Parliament voted to substantially weaken corporate sustainability rules and green investments, exempting over 80% of companies from due diligence requirements, in favor of rearmament and economic competitiveness priorities.

This trend has redefined sustainability itself. ESG funds that once excluded weapon manufacturers on ethical grounds are now promoting "defense funds" framed around protecting freedom and democracy. Similarly, the British government has encouraged private investors to reassess defense as a positive ESG category. Overall, rising polarization, particularly in Europe following the Russia-Ukraine war as well as the Israel-U.S.-Iran war, has enabled political and business actors to reshape CSR and ESG frameworks to morally legitimize investments in the arms industry, long regarded as a "sin industry" and excluded by sustainable investors.

The instrumentalization of CSR for political purposes is not a new phenomenon. In autocratic contexts such as China or in many African countries, CSR has often been used to strengthen governmental relations and fulfill political rather than social objectives. What is new is the growing reconceptualization of CSR in democratic contexts to serve national and geopolitical interests rather than universal social or environmental goals as well as the concern that elites in these countries have been more accepting of autocratization and democratic backsliding to serve geopolitical interests.

The consequence of these developments is that the intersection and repercussions of societal polarization, politicization, and securitization are fragmenting CSR itself: its overall meaning and scope, its broader role in guiding business's place in society, and the way CSR is being strategized and operationalized by business firms. As corporations realign around national interests rather than universal norms, CSR is becoming more diverse and context-specific, leading to divergent approaches shaped by geopolitical and domestic political factors. These emerging CSR models remain poorly understood. Against this backdrop, this special issue is guided by the overarching question: What does Corporate Social Responsibility entail in times of societal polarization, politicization, and securitization?

Potential topics

  • What responsibilities do firms assume when navigating heightened political and societal tensions?
  • What does "responsible" corporate behavior mean in today's polarized global political economy?
  • How is CSR evolving to address the complex moral and strategic challenges of an increasingly divided world?
  • Do corporations counter populist and illiberal politics, or primarily align with dominant power structures?
  • How do firms recalibrate ESG and CSR commitments while maintaining legitimacy across diverse stakeholders?
  • Which role does CSR play in specific industries such as defense industrial complex, including defense-focused tech firms?
  • To what extent has CSR enabled corporate political activity (CPA) that influences democratic governance in ways that advance corporate interests?
  • How do new forms of "reverse CSR" or politically adaptive responsibility emerge?
  • How does the geographical context influence the conceptualization of CSR?
  • Is CSR diffusing from autocratic to democratic contexts as a tool of political signaling rather than social progress?
  • How do the underlying philosophical and epistemological assumptions of CSR differ across contexts?
  • How can established theoretical perspectives account for geopolitically fragmented CSR models?
  • How can nationalistic or "Western populist" CSR be conceptualized in a priori democratic contexts?
  • What theoretical frameworks need to be developed to account for the instrumentalization of CSR for national and geopolitical purposes?
  • Which role does CSR play in contexts of violent conflict?
  • How do security demands shape CSR's definition and scope?
  • What new priorities emerge when CSR is applied in the defense industry, particularly regarding process vs. product dimensions?
  • How do polarization, politicization, and securitization collectively shape CSR trajectories, and what role do businesses, governments, and other stakeholders play?
  • How do businesses weigh and prioritize imperatives posed by polarization, politicization, and securitization, and how does this influence their CSR agendas?
  • How do businesses recalibrate their CSR strategies to account for new and competing societal priorities?
  • How do governments integrate these dynamics when devising or revising CSR regulations?
  • Do we see emerging surveillance states arising from mutually beneficial collaborations between the defense-industrial complex (including tech firms) and governments?
  • Do we observe any sidelining or dismantling of international institutions and cooperation structures established after the Second World War?
  • How do societal stakeholders navigate this nexus when formulating expectations towards businesses and exerting pressure?

  • October 5, 2026: Online pre-submission workshop (participation optional)
  • August 1, 2027: Submission window opens
  • August 31, 2027: Submission window closes

item.title: The Disinformation Economy: Digital Markets of Influence, Conflict, and Polarization
item.content:encoded:
Carlos Diaz Ruiz, Hanken School of Economics

Sofia Ulver, Lund University

James Pamment, Lund University

The online information landscape is a site for contested ideas, but it is also a marketplace; under the platform economy, every engagement has monetary value. This setup encourages content creators to circulate the kinds of material most likely to capture attention, even if it is incendiary. Central to this business model are the algorithmic recommendation systems, which are designed to monetize attention while simultaneously amplifying disinformation.

The term "Disinformation Economy" was introduced in a report published by the McCain Institute and The Carter Center. It highlights how the sources circulating disinformation extract financial benefits from digital marketing infrastructures, particularly through the architecture of advertising technologies (AdTech). Researchers estimate that 1.68% of digital advertising budgets are redirected to fake news websites, amounting to approximately US$2.4 billion in the US alone and nearly US$6 billion worldwide. This figure suggests that brands are inadvertently funding fake news and disinformation with their budgets.

The special issue aims to extend existing research on how platform architectures monetize and, at times, underwrite the spread of online disinformation, incentivizing the production of fake news websites, and the circulation of incendiary content through the creator economy. Although we know that polarization thrives in the online "conflict markets" designed to reward click maximization, we do not know well whether influencers profiting from radicalizing content is a likely outcome of the system or a regrettable side effect.

Policymakers increasingly recognize that malicious actors exploit digital advertising infrastructures to undermine democratic institutions and divide society, quickly becoming "hybrid threats," which is when state or non-state actors seek to exploit the vulnerabilities of democracies to their own advantage while remaining below the threshold of formal warfare. For instance, the infrastructures of the advertising market allow "dark money" actors to run influence campaigns unchecked. A recent report by the Swedish Psychological Defense Agency illustrates the emergence of a hybrid organization that applies digital marketing tools to conduct state-sponsored influence operations. And yet, we do not know to what extent influence operations co-opt malpractice in digital marketing.

This special issue invites contributions that seek to conceptualize and theorize disinformation research at the intersection of business, marketing, and society. However, we believe that it is insufficient merely to appreciate the problem; instead, we call for research that dares to find solutions that can inform public policy, change managerial practice, and strengthen society. We welcome contributions that can enhance social resilience against the spread of disinformation online.

We approach disinformation broadly, incorporating not just falsehoods but also dual-use technologies (like AI-generated synthetic media like deepfakes), which can disrupt social realities. Critical researchers on marketing and consumer research have shown that the accelerating speed of automation, big data, and algorithmic intensification give rise to new "manufactured consumers", becoming an ever more fragmented, yet controlable, societal formation. Thus, we would need to know more about how disinformation, scams, and fraud have become integral to the ebbs and flows of a digitally mediated consumer culture.

Multidisciplinary research contributions from across business disciplines, media studies, the social sciences, and public policy are welcome. We are particularly interested in research that addresses marketing technologies and practices in connection to disinformation. Other relevant research areas include understanding and countering deceptive online practices such as fake news, enhancing resilience through media literacy, fact-checking, platform governance, platform economies, and critical disinformation studies.

Potential topics

  • Whether and how programmatic advertising funds fake news?
  • How do the recommender algorithms amplify incendiary content?
  • How can AI-generated content be used to spread disinformation?
  • Do the monetization schemes of the creator economy reward polarization?
  • How do influence operations exploit marketing infrastructures?
  • What initiatives and interventions can strengthen societal resilience to disinformation?
  • What forms of platform governance can protect liberal deliberative democracies?
  • What methodologies, including Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT), can be used to investigate disinformation on AdTech and social media?

Timeline

  • September 15, 2026: Manuscript deadline
